## Choosing a display for the data {.ojs-slide .example #chart-choice}

::: {.lede-min}
Tick the display that suits each set of data. The reasoning appears underneath.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Short labels so all five fit on ONE line at 21px. The fuller names
// (stem-and-leaf, pie) live in the reasoning underneath, where there is room.
ccOpts = ["Bar or pie", "Histogram", "Scatter plot", "Time series", "Box plot"]

// Exercise 1 of the beamer Seminar 1, answers and reasoning carried over.
ccQ = [
  {q: "The tax paid by a light engineering company and its annual profit, for 20 consecutive years.",
   a: "Scatter plot",
   hint: "Look again at how many measures there are, and at what pairs them up.",
   why: "A scatter plot shows the relationship between the two numerical variables. Each of the twenty years supplies one pair of observations."},
  {q: "The types of premises occupied by all the small businesses in a town: office, factory, warehouse, and so on.",
   a: "Bar or pie",
   hint: "Ask first whether any of this can go on a number line at all.",
   why: "The variable is categorical. A bar chart or pie chart compares the counts in each category."},
  {q: "The salary of a trainee accountant in the first year of training, at 30 major accountancy firms.",
   a: "Histogram",
   hint: "One measure, thirty values of it, and the shape is what you are after.",
   why: "A histogram shows the distribution of one numerical variable. A stem-and-leaf plot also shows the distribution and preserves the individual values."},
  {q: "The number of trainee accountants enrolling for professional examinations each year since 1960.",
   a: "Time series",
   hint: "Consider how the year relates to the recorded enrolment.",
   why: "A time series plot shows how enrolment changes from year to year."},
  {q: "The years of experience and the current salary of a random sample of economists at a New York bank.",
   a: "Scatter plot",
   hint: "Count the measures recorded for each economist.",
   why: "Two numerical measures per person, so each economist is one point."}
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// What each display is FOR. A wrong answer is explained by naming the job the
// chosen chart actually does, which is one line per option rather than one
// per (question, wrong option) pair — twenty of those would say the same five
// things over and over.
ccJob = ({
  "Bar or pie":   "A bar or pie chart compares counts across named categories",
  "Histogram":    "A histogram shows the shape of one numerical measure",
  "Scatter plot": "A scatter plot shows how two numerical measures move together",
  "Time series":  "A time series plot follows one measure against time",
  "Box plot":     "A box plot summarises the spread of one numerical measure"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Every example plot is real worksheet data, so the picture a student sees
// here is one they meet again later in the module:
//   R&D spend            Seminar 1, Exercise 3   (also slides 8 and 9)
//   Executive pay        Seminar 1, Exercise 2
//   Executive salaries   Seminar 1, Exercise 4   (the stem-and-leaf one)
//   Y against X          Seminar 8, Exercise 2
//   Monthly demand       Seminar 9, Exercise 1
ccStyle = ({fontSize: "13px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
            color: "#6E7681", background: "transparent"})

ccRD = [6.0, 10.4, 10.5, 9.0, 7.3, 6.6, 6.9, 8.2, 7.1, 8.1,
        7.9, 6.8, 7.4, 9.5, 8.1, 13.5, 9.9, 6.9, 11.1, 8.2,
        8.0, 7.7, 7.4, 6.5, 9.5, 8.2, 6.9, 7.2, 8.2, 6.7]

ccSalary = [846, 457, 563, 1466, 1200, 2164, 746, 1611, 824, 824, 1310,
            1007, 1367, 575, 1252, 1354, 2479, 1238, 927, 1253, 925,
            1284, 1279, 1660, 860]

// Five of the twenty-six, all with SHORT names. The bar chart is the only
// plot with words on its y axis, so it used to set the shared left margin at
// 88 — which left the other four, and the box plot worst of all, with a band
// of empty space down their left side and the drawing pushed off centre.
// Picking short names lets every plot share a 44px margin instead.
ccPay = [["CBS", 60.25], ["Exxon", 34.90], ["AT&T", 21.00],
         ["Apple", 4.17], ["Tesco", 1.90]].map(([k, v]) => ({k, v}))

ccPairs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].map((x, i) => ({x, y: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128][i]}))

ccMonths = [23, 39, 36, 26, 36, 12, 26, 30, 42, 35, 36, 28]
  .map((x, i) => ({month: i + 1, x}))

// One geometry for all five: identical margins mean the axes are the same
// length and the ticks the same size from plot to plot, so clicking between
// displays changes the picture and nothing else. marginLeft is set by the
// longest company name on the bar chart; the numeric plots spend that space
// on their y-axis label.
ccBase = ({
  width: 400, height: 152,
  marginTop: 10, marginRight: 16, marginBottom: 56, marginLeft: 66,
  style: ccStyle
})

// labelOffset 38 against a 48 bottom margin: Plot's default sets the axis
// label directly under the tick text and the two touched.
// The two labelOffsets are not equal because they are not measured the same
// way: Plot pushes the x label DOWN from the axis and the y label LEFT from
// it, past tick text of different lengths. These two land both labels the
// same distance clear of their tick numbers, which is what reads as even.
ccAxX = (label) => ({label, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 46, tickSize: 5})
ccAxY = (label, ticks, domain) => ({label, labelAnchor: "center",
                                    labelOffset: 55, tickSize: 5,
                                    ticks, domain, grid: true})
// Explicit tick values, not a count. The shared geometry leaves a 94px plot
// area and `ticks: n` is only a HINT — d3 rounds to a nice step, so both 4
// and 5 came back with six labels 15px apart under 13px type, all but
// touching, while leaving it automatic dropped to two. Naming the values is
// the only way to fix the pitch, and these datasets never change.

ccDemo = ({
  "Bar or pie": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: ccAxX("Executive pay ($m)"),
    y: {label: null, tickSize: 5},
    marks: [
      Plot.barX(ccPay, {y: "k", x: "v", fill: "#325D88",
        sort: {y: "x", reverse: true}}),
      Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#B0B7C0"})
    ]}),
  "Histogram": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: ccAxX("R&D spend (% of revenue)"),
    y: ccAxY("Firms", [0, 4, 8]),
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(ccRD, Plot.binX({y: "count"},
        {x: d => d, thresholds: d3.range(6, 15), fill: "#325D88"})),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#B0B7C0"})
    ]}),
  "Scatter plot": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: ccAxX("X"), y: ccAxY("Y", [0, 40, 80, 120]),
    marks: [Plot.dot(ccPairs, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "#325D88", r: 3.4})]}),
  "Time series": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: {...ccAxX("Month"), tickFormat: "d"}, // From zero: a demand axis that starts at 15 exaggerates every dip.
    y: ccAxY("Demand", [0, 25, 50], [0, 50]),
    marks: [Plot.line(ccMonths, {x: "month", y: "x",
      stroke: "#325D88", strokeWidth: 2})]}),
  "Box plot": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: {...ccAxX("Executive salary (£000s)"), grid: true},
    y: {label: null, ticks: [], tickSize: 5},
    marks: [Plot.boxX(ccSalary, {x: d => d, fill: "#CBD9E6", stroke: "#325D88"})]})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ccIcon = {
  const NAVY = "#325D88";
  const wrap = inner =>
    `<svg width="42" height="26" viewBox="0 0 42 26" aria-hidden="true">${inner}</svg>`;
  // Bars on a 40-wide strip sitting on a baseline at y = 22. A histogram's
  // bars touch and a bar chart's do not, which is the one difference a
  // student is meant to read off these thumbnails.
  const bars = (hs, pitch, w) => hs.map((h, i) =>
    `<rect x="${2 + i * pitch}" y="${22 - h}" width="${w}" height="${h}" fill="${NAVY}"/>`
  ).join("");
  const line = (x1, y1, x2, y2) =>
    `<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="1.6"/>`;
  return ({
    "Bar or pie": wrap(bars([16, 9, 13, 6], 10, 7)),
    "Histogram": wrap(bars([5, 12, 18, 11, 5], 8, 8)),
    "Scatter plot": wrap([[5,20],[11,16],[16,18],[21,13],[26,11],[32,8],[38,5]]
      .map(([x, y]) => `<circle cx="${x}" cy="${y}" r="2.1" fill="${NAVY}"/>`).join("")),
    "Time series": wrap(
      `<polyline points="3,20 10,12 17,16 24,7 31,11 39,4" fill="none"
         stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/>`),
    "Box plot": wrap(line(3, 13, 12, 13) + line(28, 13, 39, 13) +
      `<rect x="12" y="7" width="16" height="12" fill="none" stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="1.6"/>` +
      line(21, 7, 21, 19))
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ccI = Inputs.radio([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], {value: 1, label: "Question"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ccPrompt = html`<div class="quiz-q">${ccQ[ccI - 1].q}</div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ccPick = {
  ccI;   // naming it here rebuilds the input when the question changes, which
         // is the only way to clear the previous answer's ticks
  // html([...]) rather than html`...`: the sketch is a string of markup and
  // the tagged form would escape it into visible angle brackets.
  // radio, not checkbox: every question has exactly one right display, so
  // letting the room tick three of them only invites a wrong kind of answer.
  return Inputs.radio(ccOpts, {
    label: "Suitable display",
    format: v => html([`<span class="quiz-opt">${ccIcon[v]}<span>${v}</span></span>`])
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ccFeedback = {
  const want = ccQ[ccI - 1].a;
  if (!ccPick) return html`<div class="quiz-fb quiz-idle">Pick a display to see the reasoning.</div>`;
  const ok = ccPick === want;
  // A wrong pick names the job the chosen chart does and points back at the
  // data. It does NOT name the answer: handing it over ends the thinking, and
  // the radio is still there to try again with.
  const text = ok
    ? html`<b>Yes.</b> ${ccQ[ccI - 1].why}`
    : html`<b>Not quite.</b> ${ccJob[ccPick]}. ${ccQ[ccI - 1].hint}`;
  // The plot always shows the display that was PICKED, not the right one —
  // on a wrong answer it is the thing they asked for, which is an argument
  // rather than a giveaway.
  return html`<div class="quiz-answer">
    <div class="quiz-fb ${ok ? "quiz-ok" : "quiz-no"}">${text}</div>
    <figure class="quiz-plot">
      <figcaption>${ccPick}</figcaption>
      ${ccDemo[ccPick]()}
    </figure>
  </div>`;
}
```

Descriptive statistics

Each summary from the previous slide can be calculated with one line of R.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
pay <- c(38, 42, 45, 47, 49, 50,
         50, 50, 52, 54, 56, 59, 
         62)

# Descriptive statistics
sort(table(pay), decreasing = TRUE)[1] # mode
range(pay)   # 38 and 62
median(pay)  # the 7th value once sorted
mean(pay)    # 654 / 13
var(pay)     # divisor is n - 1, not n
sd(pay)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
Change the last salary to `96` and run it again. The mode and median stay the same in this example. The mean and standard deviation change because they depend on the size of the last salary.
:::

## Sampling a Distribution Randomly {.formula-slide #sampling-formal}

::: {.lede-min}
In survey sampling, we draw a small random sample from a larger population. Distinguish the population quantities from the corresponding sample quantities.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.fragment}
[Population]{.col-head}
[Large, size $\color{#325D88}{N}$]{.col-sub}

$$\begin{gathered} \{x_1, \dots, x_{\color{#325D88}{N}}\} \\[4pt] \color{#B94A48}{\mu} = \frac{1}{\color{#325D88}{N}} \sum_{j=1}^{\color{#325D88}{N}} x_j \qquad \color{#F47C3C}{\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{\color{#325D88}{N}} \sum_{j=1}^{\color{#325D88}{N}} (x_j - \color{#B94A48}{\mu})^2 \end{gathered}$$

These are fixed population quantities that we want to estimate. Equivalently $\color{#F47C3C}{\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{N}\sum x_j^2 - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}^2$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Sample]{.col-head}
[Small, size $\color{#F47C3C}{n}$]{.col-sub}

$$\begin{gathered} \{X_1, \dots, X_{\color{#F47C3C}{n}}\} \\[4pt] \color{#F47C3C}{\bar X} = \frac{1}{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} X_i \qquad \color{#F47C3C}{\widehat{\sigma}^{2}} = \frac{1}{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} (X_i - \color{#F47C3C}{\bar X})^2 \end{gathered}$$

These quantities can be calculated from the sample and vary from one sample to another. R's `var()` gives $s^2$, which divides by $n - 1$ instead and removes a small bias.
:::
::::

::: {.note-box .fragment}
There are $\binom{N}{n}$ possible samples of size $n$. **Simple random sampling** (without replacement) makes each one equally likely.
:::

## Three Properties of the Sample Mean {.qcard-slide #xbar-properties}

::: {.lede-min}
The sample mean $\bar X$ changes from sample to sample, so it is itself a random variable; the number you compute from your data is its value, $\bar x$. The following properties describe its use as an estimator of $\mu$.
:::

:::: {.prop-grid}

::: {.prop-card .prop-unbiased .fragment}
[Unbiased]{.prop-name}

[$\operatorname{E}[\bar X] = \mu$]{.prop-math}

[Its expected value equals the population mean.]{.prop-q}
:::

::: {.prop-card .prop-efficient .fragment}
[Efficient]{.prop-name}

[$\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N - n}{N - 1}$]{.prop-math}

[The smallest variance of any unbiased weighted average.]{.prop-q}
:::

::: {.prop-card .prop-consistent .fragment}
[Consistent]{.prop-name}

[$\bar X \to \mu \;\text{ as }\; n \to N$]{.prop-math}

[The estimate approaches $\mu$ as $n$ increases; at $n = N$ it equals $\mu$.]{.prop-q}
:::

::::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Drawn without replacement, the $X_i$ are not independent, and that shrinks the variance by $\frac{N - n}{N - 1}$, the finite population correction. When $N \gg n$ it is close to 1, so $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) \approx \sigma^2/n$, the formula the intervals use.
:::

## Proving Unbiasedness {.formula-slide #xbar-proof}

::: {.lede-min}
Draw $X_1, \dots, X_n$ without replacement from $N$ units $x_1, \dots, x_N$. Each unit is equally likely to be the $i$-th draw, so $P(X_i = x_j) = 1/N$.
:::

$$\textstyle \operatorname{E}[X_i] \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{N} x_j\, P(X_i = x_j) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{N} x_j \cdot \frac{1}{N} \;=\; \color{#B94A48}{\mu}$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [The same sum with $(x_j - \mu)^2$ gives $\operatorname{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2$. Now average the $n$ draws]{.deriv-note}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\textstyle \operatorname{E}[\bar X] \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{E}[X_i] \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\, n\mu \;=\; \color{#B94A48}{\mu} \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{unbiased}}$$
:::

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Why the second step needs no independence]{.deriv-note}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\textstyle \operatorname{E}[X + Y] = \sum (x + y)\, P(x, y) = \sum x\, P(x) + \sum y\, P(y) = \operatorname{E}[X] + \operatorname{E}[Y]$$
:::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Only each variable's own probabilities appear, never $P(x, y) = P(x)\,P(y)$, so $\operatorname{E}[\bar X] = \mu$ with or without replacement.
:::

## Proving the Variance and Consistency {.formula-slide #xbar-proof-var}

::: {.lede-min}
With replacement the draws are independent: $P(X_2 = x_l \mid X_1 = x_k) = 1/N$. Without, it is $1/(N-1)$ or 0, so let $c = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$.
:::

$$\textstyle 0 \;=\; \operatorname{Var}(X_1 + \dots + X_N) \;=\; N\sigma^2 + N(N-1)\,c \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; c = -\frac{\sigma^2}{N-1}$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [At $n = N$ the total is fixed, which determines the covariance. The same expansion for $n$ draws]{.deriv-note}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\textstyle \operatorname{Var}(\bar X) \;=\; \frac{1}{n^2}\Big[\, n\sigma^2 - n(n-1)\frac{\sigma^2}{N-1} \Big] \;=\; \color{#325D88}{\frac{\sigma^2}{n} \cdot \frac{N-n}{N-1}}$$
:::

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Chebyshev, $P(|Y - \operatorname{E}[Y]| \ge \varepsilon) \le \operatorname{Var}(Y)/\varepsilon^2$, with $Y = \bar X$]{.deriv-note}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\textstyle P\big(|\bar X - \mu| \ge \varepsilon\big) \;\le\; \frac{\sigma^2}{n\,\varepsilon^2} \cdot \frac{N-n}{N-1} \;\to\; 0 \;\text{ as }\; n \to N \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{consistent}}$$
:::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
The factor is 1 with replacement ($c = 0$) or at $n = 1$; close to 1 when $N \gg n$.
:::

## The Sample Variance {.formula-slide #sample-var}

::: {.lede-min}
The hat marks an estimate: $\widehat{\sigma}^{2}$ is the population formula run on the sample, so it is random. Is its expected value equal to $\sigma^2$?
:::

$$\textstyle \widehat{\sigma}^{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2 \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 \;-\; \bar X^2$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Take expectations with $\operatorname{E}[Y^2] = \operatorname{Var}(Y) + \operatorname{E}[Y]^2$, for $Y = X_i$ and for $Y = \bar X$]{.deriv-note}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\textstyle \operatorname{E}[\widehat{\sigma}^{2}] \;=\; (\sigma^2 + \color{#B94A48}{\mu}^2) \;-\; \Big(\frac{\sigma^2}{n} \cdot \frac{N-n}{N-1} + \color{#B94A48}{\mu}^2\Big) \;=\; \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{N(n-1)}{n(N-1)}$$
:::

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Biased, a little below $\sigma^2$. Rescale; as $N \to \infty$ this is $s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (X_i - \bar X)^2$]{.deriv-note}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\textstyle \operatorname{E}\Big[\frac{n(N-1)}{N(n-1)}\, \widehat{\sigma}^{2}\Big] \;=\; \color{#325D88}{\sigma^2} \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{unbiased}}$$
:::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
So the unknown $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)$ can be estimated from the data by $\widehat{\sigma}^{2}\, \frac{N-n}{N(n-1)}$.
:::

## Normal Approximation to the Distribution of $\bar X$ {.formula-slide #xbar-normal}

::: {.lede-min}
By the CLT, for large $n$ the sample mean is close to normal, with spread the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ (taking $N \gg n$).
:::

::: {.fragment}
[The approximation]{.col-head}
[Centre $\mu$, spread $\sigma/\sqrt n$]{.col-sub}

$$\bar X \approx N\Big(\color{#B94A48}{\mu}, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\Big) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \frac{\bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \approx N(0, 1) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; P\Big(\frac{\bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \le a\Big) \to \Phi(a)$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[How close is $\bar X$ to $\mu$?]{.col-head}
[Divide every side by $\sigma/\sqrt n$]{.col-sub}

$$P(|\bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}| < \varepsilon) = P\Big({-\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}{\sigma}} < Z < \frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}{\sigma}\Big) = \Phi\Big(\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}{\sigma}\Big) - \Phi\Big({-\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}{\sigma}}\Big)$$
:::

::: {.fragment}

## A Confidence Interval for $\mu$ {.formula-slide #ci-derive}

::: {.lede-min}
A $(1 - \alpha)$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is a **random interval**, centred at $\bar X$, that contains $\mu$ with probability $1 - \alpha$. The derivation is below.
:::

$$\textstyle P\big(-q \le \bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu} \le q\big) \;=\; 1 - \alpha$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Divide by the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$; the cut-off becomes $z_{\alpha/2}$, with $\Phi(z_{\alpha/2}) = 1 - \alpha/2$]{.deriv-note}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\textstyle P\Big(-z_{\alpha/2} \le \frac{\bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \le z_{\alpha/2}\Big) \;=\; 1 - \alpha$$
:::

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Multiply through by $\sigma/\sqrt n$ and rearrange around $\mu$]{.deriv-note}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\textstyle P\Big(\bar X - z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \;\le\; \color{#B94A48}{\mu} \;\le\; \bar X + z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\Big) \;=\; 1 - \alpha$$
:::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
So $\bar X \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n$ is the interval; for 95%, $\alpha = 0.05$ and $z_{0.025} = 1.96$.
:::

## Calculating a confidence interval {.stage-slide #cieq-formula}

::: {.lede-min}
Example: $\sigma = 15$ is known, and a sample of $n = 25$ gives $\bar x = 103.2$. Build the 95% interval.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="cieq-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cieq-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cieq-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cieq-frag-3"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cieq-frag-4"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Before sampling, $\bar X \pm 5.88$ is random and contains $\mu$ with probability 0.95. Once we observe $\bar x = 103.2$, $(97.32, 109.08)$ is fixed: it contains $\mu$ or it does not. The 95% describes the method across repeated samples.
:::

## From the sampling distribution to an interval {.stage-slide #ciflip-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
To see why it works, use $\mu = 100$ for illustration. In practice, $\mu$ is unknown.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="ciflip-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="ciflip-frag-1" data-fragment-index="1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="ciflip-frag-2" data-fragment-index="2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="ciflip-frag-3" data-fragment-index="3"}

::: {.slide-footer .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
$\bar x \pm 5.88$ contains $\mu$ exactly when $\bar x$ falls within 5.88 of $\mu$, which happens 95% of the time.
:::

## Interpreting a confidence interval {.stage-slide #ci-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-ci}
<div id="ci-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

:::: {.claim-pair}

::: {.claim-cell .claim-wrong}
[Tempting]{.claim-tag}

"**My** interval contains $\mu$ with 95% probability."
:::

::: {.claim-cell .claim-right}
[Correct]{.claim-tag}

"95% of intervals **built this way** contain $\mu$."
:::

## Simulate the Sample Mean and Its Interval {.ojs-slide #ci-lab}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof clIn = Inputs.form({
  n: Inputs.range([2, 200], {value: 10, step: 1, label: html`Sample size <i style="text-transform: none">n</i>`}),
  conf: Inputs.range([0.8, 0.99], {value: 0.95, step: 0.01, label: "Confidence"}),
  rule: Inputs.radio(["Known σ: x̄ ± z·σ/√n", "Unknown σ: x̄ ± z·s/√n", "Unknown σ: x̄ ± t·s/√n"], {value: "Known σ: x̄ ± z·σ/√n", label: "Interval"}),
  again: Inputs.button("New samples")
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="cl-dials">${ins.n}${ins.conf}${ins.again}</div><div class="cl-dials cl-rule">${ins.rule}</div>`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// The t quantile is exact: the regularized incomplete beta (Numerical Recipes'
// continued fraction) inverted by bisection. It matches R's qt() to 4 places
// for df from 1 to 100, so the t row agrees with the table on the worksheet.
clLgam = x => { const c = [76.18009172947146, -86.50532032941677, 24.01409824083091,
    -1.231739572450155, 0.1208650973866179e-2, -0.5395239384953e-5];
  let y = x, t = x + 5.5, s = 1.000000000190015; t -= (x + 0.5) * Math.log(t);
  for (const ci of c) s += ci / ++y;
  return -t + Math.log(2.5066282746310005 * s / x); }
clBetacf = (a, b, x) => { let c = 1, d = 1 / (1 - (a + b) * x / (a + 1)), h = d;
  for (let m = 1; m < 200; m++) { const m2 = 2 * m;
    let aa = m * (b - m) * x / ((a + m2 - 1) * (a + m2));
    d = 1 / (1 + aa * d); c = 1 + aa / c; h *= d * c;
    aa = -(a + m) * (a + b + m) * x / ((a + m2) * (a + m2 + 1));
    d = 1 / (1 + aa * d); c = 1 + aa / c; const del = d * c; h *= del;
    if (Math.abs(del - 1) < 1e-12) break; }
  return h; }
clIbeta = (a, b, x) => { if (x <= 0) return 0; if (x >= 1) return 1;
  const bt = Math.exp(clLgam(a + b) - clLgam(a) - clLgam(b) + a * Math.log(x) + b * Math.log(1 - x));
  return x < (a + 1) / (a + b + 2) ? bt * clBetacf(a, b, x) / a : 1 - bt * clBetacf(b, a, 1 - x) / b; }
clTcdf = (t, df) => { const p = 0.5 * clIbeta(df / 2, 0.5, df / (df + t * t)); return t > 0 ? 1 - p : p; }
clInv = cdf => p => { let lo = 0, hi = 1000;
  for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) { const m = (lo + hi) / 2; cdf(m) < p ? lo = m : hi = m; }
  return (lo + hi) / 2; }
clMu = 100
clSd = 15
clReps = 2000
// Seeded from the button count, so moving the confidence slider or the
// interval rule re-draws the SAME samples: only the intervals change.
clSim = {
  const n = clIn.n, rnd = d3.randomNormal.source(d3.randomLcg(((clIn.again + 1) * 0.6180339887) % 1))(clMu, clSd);
  const xbar = [], s = [], row = new Float64Array(n);
  for (let r = 0; r < clReps; r++) {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) row[i] = rnd();
    xbar.push(d3.mean(row)); s.push(d3.deviation(row));
  }
  return {n, xbar, s};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const {n, xbar, s} = clSim, p = (1 + clIn.conf) / 2, rn = Math.sqrt(n);
  const crit = clIn.rule === "Unknown σ: x̄ ± t·s/√n" ? clInv(t => clTcdf(t, n - 1))(p) : clInv(Phi)(p);
  const half = xbar.map((_, r) => crit * (clIn.rule === "Known σ: x̄ ± z·σ/√n" ? clSd : s[r]) / rn);
  const hit = xbar.map((x, r) => Math.abs(x - clMu) <= half[r]);
  const cover = d3.mean(hit, h => +h);
  const style = ({fontSize: "14px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"});
  const T = d3.range(clMu - 25, clMu + 25.01, 1);
  const dist = Plot.plot({
    width: 490, height: 245, marginLeft: 12, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style,
    x: {domain: [clMu - 25, clMu + 25], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {axis: null, insetTop: 18},   // headroom so the peak clears the title
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(xbar, Plot.binX({y: "proportion"}, {x: d => d, thresholds: T, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5})),
      Plot.ruleX([clMu], {stroke: "#3E3F3A", strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim}),
      Plot.text(["Means of 2,000 samples from N(100, 15²)"], {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -30, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.navy, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16})
    ]
  });
  const idx = d3.range(50);
  const ints = Plot.plot({
    width: 490, height: 245, marginLeft: 12, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style,
    x: {domain: [clMu - 30, clMu + 30], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [-1, 50], axis: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY(idx, {y: i => i, x1: i => xbar[i] - half[i], x2: i => xbar[i] + half[i], clip: true,
        stroke: i => hit[i] ? "#9FB6CC" : PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(idx, {y: i => i, x: i => xbar[i], r: 1.8, fill: i => hit[i] ? PPAL.navy : PPAL.brick}),
      Plot.text(["The first 50 intervals"], {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -30, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.navy, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16}),
      Plot.ruleX([clMu], {stroke: "#3E3F3A", strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 4"})
    ]
  });
  const f = (v, k = 2) => v.toFixed(k);
  // The verdict reads the run, so it changes as the controls do.
  const pct = v => `<b>${f(100 * v, 1)}%</b>`, target = `${Math.round(100 * clIn.conf)}%`;
  const verdict = (n, c) => clIn.rule === "Unknown σ: x̄ ± z·s/√n" && c < clIn.conf - 0.02
    ? `With s in place of σ and n = ${n}, the z cut-off is too narrow: only ${pct(c)} of the intervals contain μ, not ${target}. <b>Switch to t</b> to account for uncertainty in the estimate of σ.`
    : `The mean X̄ centres on μ (<b>unbiased</b>) and its variance σ²/n shrinks as n grows (<b>consistent</b>). ${pct(c)} of the intervals contain μ, close to the specified ${target} confidence level.`;
  return html`<div class="cr-row">${dist}${ints}</div>
  <div class="ojs-eq cl-stats">
    <span>Mean of <span class="cl-bar">X</span> ≈ ${f(d3.mean(xbar))} <span class="na-note">(μ = ${clMu})</span></span>
    <span>Var(<span class="cl-bar">X</span>) ≈ <span class="cl-navy">${f(d3.variance(xbar))}</span> <span class="na-note">(σ²/n = ${f(clSd ** 2 / n)})</span></span>
    <span>Coverage = <span class="${Math.abs(cover - clIn.conf) < 0.02 ? "hit" : "miss"}">${f(100 * cover, 1)}%</span> <span class="na-note">(cut-off ${f(crit, 3)})</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">${verdict(n, cover)}</div>`;
}
```

## Forty Punts {.formula-slide .example #punt-clt}

::: {.lede-min}
An NFL punter has historically averaged 41 yards a punt, with a standard deviation of 8 yards. What is the probability that their next 40 punts average at least 45 yards?
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.fragment}
[The average of 40 punts]{.col-head}
[Its centre and its standard error]{.col-sub}

$$\begin{gathered} \bar X_{40} = \frac{1}{40}\sum_{i=1}^{40} X_i \\ \operatorname{E}[\bar X_{40}] = \color{#B94A48}{41} \qquad \operatorname{SD}(\bar X_{40}) = \frac{8}{\sqrt{40}} = 1.26 \end{gathered}$$

::: {.fragment}
[By the CLT]{.col-head}
[Standardise, then read the table]{.col-sub}

$$\begin{aligned} P(\bar X_{40} \ge 45) &= P\Big(\frac{\bar X_{40} - 41}{8/\sqrt{40}} \ge \frac{45 - 41}{8/\sqrt{40}}\Big) \\ &= P(Z \ge 3.16) = 1 - \Phi(3.16) \\ &= 7.8 \times 10^{-4} \end{aligned}$$

About 1 in 1,300. Forty punts averaging 45 yards would be **3.16 standard errors** above the punter's history.
:::
